title.en: The Prodigal Son and the Rich Father (Lotus Sutra)
title.zh: 窮子喻：長者與失散之子（法華經）

region.en: The Buddhist assembly at Vulture Peak, told within the world of merchants and provinces (symbolic pin — Ganges valley)
region.zh: 靈鷲山法會所說，寓於商旅與諸國之世界（象徵性定位——恆河流域）

texts.period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: A man's son runs away in childhood and is lost for fifty years; the father, grown immensely rich, refuses to force himself on the terrified, ragged son who appears at his gate, but hires him dirt-cheap to shovel dung for twenty years, slowly raises him to stewardship, and on his deathbed reveals to the assembled kin: this is my son, all my wealth is his. Mahakasyapa and the three elders confess themselves the prodigals: the Tathagata knew their Buddha-nature all along but soothed their low disposition with the modest Nirvana of discipleship, until they woke to find themselves heirs to the treasure of Buddha-knowledge they never sought.
summary.zh: 有人之子幼年逃走，失散五十年；父成巨富，見襤褸之子懼逃於門前，不即相認，而賤值雇其運糞二十年，漸升其職，臨終當眾宣布：此吾親子，家財盡付之。大迦葉與三位長老自承即此窮子：如來早知彼等具佛種，然以其志意下劣，故以聲聞涅槃誘引之，直至其悟知自身實為如來知見大寶之繼承人——此寶從未尋求，忽然而得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); parable material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved. Comparative parallel: this lost-and-returned-son parable belongs to a cross-tradition cluster with the Gospel prodigal son (Luke 15), though the Buddhist version turns on skilful means and inheritance rather than forgiveness.

passages.text: A certain man went away from his father and lived in foreign parts for twenty, thirty, forty or fifty years, growing poor and wandering in search of food and clothing, while the father removed to another country and became a great man — rich in bullion, gems and granaries, served by slaves, elephants and carriages, doing great business in money-lending, agriculture and commerce. The father always thought of the son lost fifty years ago, pining that death might overtake him with all this wealth unused. Meanwhile the poor man, roaming through villages, towns and royal capitals, happened to reach the very town where his father lived, and saw him sitting in great pomp at his door, surrounded by brahmins, nobles and householders, dealing in hundred-thousands of gold pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. IV 'Disposition' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Terrified at the sight of so much state, the poor man fled: people like me have nothing to do here. The father recognized his son at first sight and was filled with joy, but seeing his humble disposition, he sent couriers after him only to startle him half to death — the wretched man fainted — whereupon the father sprinkled him with cold water, let him go free, and concealed from everyone that it was his son. He then practised an able device: he hired two ill-favoured men to engage the poor man for a double daily fee to help clear the heap of dirt in his house. The father himself laid off his wreath and ornaments, put on dirty raiment, took a basket, smeared himself with dust, and greeted his son from afar, telling him to stay in his service as if he were the son of the old man, and addressing him by the name of son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. IV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the son cleared the heap of dirt for twenty years, living in a hovel by the rich man's dwelling, until he felt at ease to go in and out of the mansion. The father, falling sick and feeling death near, bade the man accept his bullion and granaries; the poor man received them but still lived as poor as before, till the father saw that his son had grown able, mature, and ashamed of his former poverty. Then before the king and the gathered relations he made the announcement: this is my own son, begotten by me, lost fifty years ago; to him I leave all my revenues. The prodigal, astonished, reflected on the treasure gotten without seeking. Even so, said Mahakasyapa and the three elders, are we the sons of the Tathagata: oppressed by the three difficulties, prompted to ponder on laws like a heap of dirt, content with a poor Nirvana as our day's fee — while the Lord, knowing our strength of disposition, skilfully appointed us heirs to the treasure of the knowledge of the Tathagata, which we did not desire, nor seek, nor expect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. IV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Phantom City in the Dangerous Forest (Lotus Sutra)

region.en: A dangerous forest on the road to the Isle of Jewels, told in the Buddha's retrospective of a former Buddha-age (symbolic pin — Ganges valley)
region.zh: 通往寶處之險惡林中，佛於往劫佛世之追溯中所說（象徵性定位——恆河流域）

texts.period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: A guide leads a great caravan through a forest five hundred yojanas deep toward the Isle of Jewels; halfway, exhausted, the men beg to turn back, and the guide conjures up a magic city of repose. Once they are rested he dissolves the phantom city and tells them the true destination is near: the city was produced by magic only to give them rest. Even so, says the Buddha, the two stages of Nirvana he teaches the faint-hearted — disciples and Pratyekabuddhas — are conjured resting-places; when the travellers have halted there, the Tathagata tells them: you have not accomplished your task; the Buddha-knowledge is near.
summary.zh: 導師率大商隊穿越五百由旬險林，往寶處去；中途眾人疲極欲返，導師乃於林中化現一城，令其入城歇息。既得安樂，導師即滅化城，告眾：寶處在近，此城乃我所化，但為汝等暫得休息。佛言：如來為志弱眾生所說之二種涅槃——聲聞地、辟支佛地——亦如是化城；眾生止息其中，如來便言：汝等未辦，佛智在近。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); parable material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved. Comparative parallel: the conjured rest on an arduous journey belongs to the otherworld-voyage cluster of the wider corpus.

passages.text: By way of example, said the Buddha, suppose there is some dense forest five hundred yojanas in extent, reached by a great company of men, who have a guide to lead them on their journey to the Isle of Jewels — a guide able, clever, sagacious, well acquainted with the difficult passages of the forest. Meanwhile that great troop, tired, weary, afraid and anxious, say: 'Verily, Master, guide and leader, know that we are tired, weary, afraid and anxious; let us return; this dense forest stretches so far.' The guide, seeing them desirous of returning, thinks within himself: it ought not to be that these poor creatures should not reach that great Isle of Jewels; therefore, out of pity for them, he makes use of an artifice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. VII 'Ancient Devotion' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the middle of the forest he produces a magic city, more than a hundred or two hundred yojanas in extent, and says to the men: 'Be not afraid, do not return; there you see a populous place where you may take repose and perform all you have to do; there stay in the enjoyment of happy rest; and let him who after reposing there wants to do so, proceed on to the great Isle of Jewels.' The men in the forest are struck with astonishment: we are out of the forest, we have reached the place of happy rest — and they enter the magic city, believing they have arrived at their destination and are saved. After a while, when the guide perceives that their fatigue is gone, he causes the magic city to disappear, and says: 'Come, sirs, there you see the great Isle of Jewels quite near; as to this great city, it has been produced by me for no other purpose but to give you some repose.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. VII (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Even so, the Buddha continued, am I the Tathagata your guide and the guide of all other beings. Great is this forest of evils which must be crossed, left, shunned; it ought not to be that beings, having heard of the Buddha-knowledge, should turn back because it seems attended with too many difficulties to be gone through to the end. Knowing them feeble of character, the Tathagata, as the guide produces the magic city, very skilfully teaches two stages of Nirvana, the stage of the disciples and that of the Pratyekabuddhas, to give the creatures repose. And when they are there halting, the Tathagata himself pronounces these words: 'You have not accomplished your task, monks; you have not finished what you had to do. But behold, the Buddha-knowledge is near; what to you seems Nirvana, that is not Nirvana. Nay, it is an able device of the Tathagatas that they expound three vehicles.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. VII (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Priceless Gem Sewn in the Garment (Lotus Sutra)

region.en: The Buddhist assembly, told within the world of travellers and strange towns (symbolic pin — Ganges valley)
region.zh: 靈鷲山法會所說，寓於行旅與異鄉之世界（象徵性定位——恆河流域）

texts.period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: A man who has drunk or slept too soundly in a friend's house goes on his travels unaware that the friend has bound a priceless gem within his garment; beggared by hardship, he is content with a morsel of food until the old friend meets him and shows him the jewel he has carried all along. The five hundred Arhats confess themselves the sleeper: the Tathagata, while still treading the course of a Bodhisattva, awakened in them ideas of omniscience, but they forgot it and were content with a trifling Nirvana — until the Lord, reading their dispositions, tells them to exchange the gem and predicts their destiny to the highest enlightenment.
summary.zh: 有人醉臥或酣睡於友人之家，友人縫一無價寶珠於其衣內而去；其人不知，行旅他鄉，備嘗艱苦，得少許飲食便自足。舊友重逢，出示珠寶：此寶我久為汝繫於衣內，汝自不覺。五百羅漢自承即此醉臥者：如來昔行菩薩道時，已於我等心中植一切智之芽，我等忘之，以少分涅槃自足；如來今乃指示，並授記其必至無上菩提。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); parable material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: It is, O Lord, as if some man having come to a friend's house got drunk or fell asleep, and that friend bound a priceless gem within his garment, with the thought: let this gem be his. After a while that man rises from his seat and travels further; he goes to some other country, where he is befallen by incessant difficulties, and has great trouble to find food and clothing. By dint of great exertion he is hardly able to obtain a bit of food, with which, however, he is contented and satisfied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. VIII 'Destiny of the Five Hundred Monks' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old friend who bound that priceless gem within the man's garment happens to see him again and says: how is it, good friend, that thou hast such difficulty in seeking food and clothing, while I, in order that thou shouldst live in ease, have bound within thy garment a priceless gem, quite sufficient to fulfil all thy wishes? Go, my good friend, betake thyself, with this gem, to some great city, exchange the gem for money, and with that money do all that can be done with money. The man sees it and becomes very rich, of great power, in possession of all that the five senses can enjoy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. VIII (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the same manner, the five hundred Arhats confessed, has the Tathagata, when he still followed the course of duty of a Bodhisattva, raised in us also ideas of omniscience, but we did not perceive nor know it; we fancied that on the stage of Arhat we had reached Nirvana, and lived in difficulty because we contented ourselves with such a trifling degree of knowledge. But as our strong aspiration after the knowledge of the all-knowing has never ceased, the Tathagata teaches us the right: have no such idea of Nirvana, monks; there are in your intelligence roots of goodness which of yore I have fully developed. We confess our fault before thee; we were so childish, nescient and ignorant that we were fully contented with a small part of Nirvana under the mastership of the Sugata — unaware of the aspiration the Tathagata himself had laid in us from time immemorial.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. VIII (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dragon-Daughter who Becomes a Buddha (Lotus Sutra)

region.en: Vulture Peak, Rajagriha, and the ocean palace of the Naga-king Sagara (supernatural setting; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王舍城靈鷲山，及娑竭羅龍王之海宮（超自然場景；象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: Manjusri rises from the sea on a great lotus, and Prajnakuta challenges him: has anyone reached enlightenment in a single moment? Manjusri answers with the daughter of the Naga-king Sagara, eight years old, who has mastered a thousand meditations. Sariputra objects that no woman has ever won Buddhahood; the girl offers a gem worth the whole universe, which the Buddha accepts instantly, and in the same instant her female form vanishes, she manifests as a Bodhisattva, goes south to the world Vimala, and there shows herself a fully enlightened Tathagata preaching the law, while the worlds quake and hundreds of thousands are established on the path.
summary.zh: 文殊師利自海中乘大蓮花昇空而來。智積菩薩問：海中教化，有即身成佛者乎？文殊答以娑竭羅龍王之女，年方八歲，慧利根敏，能持諸佛法藏，於刹那頃得千三昧。舍利弗難曰：女身五礙，無成佛例。龍女即以一寶獻佛，價逾三千大千世界，佛受之；遂於眾前轉男身，即往南方無垢世界，坐寶樹下成等正覺，普為眾生說法；世界六種震動，無量眾生住不退轉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); scripture material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved. Comparative parallel: the instantaneous transformation from one form of being to Buddhahood belongs to the transformation cluster of the wider corpus.

passages.text: Manjusri, the prince royal, rose seated on a centifolious lotus, large as a carriage yoked with four horses, surrounded by many Bodhisattvas, from the bosom of the sea, from the abode of the Naga-king Sagara, and rising high into the sky went through the air to the Gridhrakuta mountain to the presence of the Lord. Prajnakuta asked how many beings he had educated during his stay in the sea; Manjusri answered: many, innumerable, incalculable — and no sooner had he spoken than thousands of lotuses rose from the bosom of the sea, bearing thousands of Bodhisattvas who flocked through the air like meteors. Asked what law he had preached there, he answered: in the bosom of the sea I have expounded the Lotus of the True Law and no other Sutra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XI 'Apparition of a Stupa' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Prajnakuta asked whether any creature was able to understand so profound a Sutra and arrive at supreme perfect enlightenment. There is, said Manjusri, the daughter of Sagara, the Naga-king, eight years old, very intelligent, of keen faculties, endowed with prudence in acts of body, speech and mind, who has caught and kept all the teachings, in substance and form, of the Tathagatas, and has acquired in one moment a thousand meditations; she is apt to display all virtues and is never deficient in them; she is fit to arrive at supreme perfect enlightenment. Prajnakuta objected: I have seen how the Lord Sakyamuni strove for enlightenment during many aeons, never slackening, until in the whole universe there was not a spot so small as a mustard-seed where he had not surrendered his body for the sake of creatures; who then would believe that she should arrive at supreme knowledge in one moment?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XI (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: At that very moment the daughter of Sagara appeared before them, saluted the Lord, and declared that she had obtained enlightenment according to her wish. Sariputra told her that supreme perfect enlightenment is not easily won: it may happen that a woman displays unflagging energy for thousands of aeons and fulfils the six perfections, but as yet there is no example of her having reached Buddhahip, because a woman cannot occupy the five ranks — of Brahma, of Indra, of a guardian of the four quarters, of a universal monarch, of a Bodhisattva incapable of sliding back. Then the girl offered the Buddha a gem which in value outweighed the whole universe, and the Lord graciously accepted it; and she asked Sariputra whether he had received it quickly. Instantly her female sex disappeared, the male sex appeared, and she manifested herself as a Bodhisattva who immediately went south to the world Vimala and there showed himself enlightened and preaching the law, filling all directions with the radiance of the thirty-two signs; all beings in the Saha-world beheld it, the worlds shook in six ways, and three thousand beings gained the acquiescence in the eternal law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XI (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Devadatta the Destroyer, Predicted to Buddhahood (Lotus Sutra)

region.en: Vulture Peak, Rajagriha, with a retrospective of a royal age long past (symbolic pin — Ganges valley)
region.zh: 王舍城靈鷲山，回溯往古轉輪王之世（象徵性定位——恆河流域）

texts.period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884 (the Devadatta section of Kern ch. XI; Kumarajiva's ch. 12)

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: The Sutra's astonishing twist on its great villain: Devadatta — in the tradition the schismatic who tried to kill the Buddha — was once the Seer who taught the Lotus of the True Law to Sakyamuni when he was a king intent on enlightenment; the king served him a full millennium, fetching grass, fuel and water and keeping his feet at night, and thus accomplished the six perfections. By the aid of Devadatta, says the Buddha, I have attained all a Tathagata's qualities; and I announce to you that this very monk Devadatta shall in an age to come become the Tathagata Devaraja, whose law shall stay twenty intermediate kalpas and whose stupa all gods and men shall worship. Whoever hears this chapter of the Sutra and trusts it has the door of the three states of misfortune shut against him.
summary.zh: 法華經於其大惡者筆下翻出奇筆：提婆達多——教史中弒佛破僧之叛徒——往昔曾為仙人，教釋迦牟尼（彼時為求道之王）法華之真法；王為其僕整一千年，取草薪汲水，夜為守足，由此圓滿六度。佛言：賴提婆達多善知識故，我得諸佛功德；今告汝等：此比丘提婆達多，過無量劫當得作佛，號天王如來，壽二十中劫，法住二十中劫，天人咸供其塔。聞此品而信受者，三惡道門閉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); scripture material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved. Comparative parallel: the enemy-as-teacher who ripens the hero's quest belongs to the boon-curse/karma-retribution cluster across the corpus.

passages.text: Of yore, monks, in times past, I have, unwearied and without repose, sought after the Sutra of the Lotus of the True Law during immense, immeasurable aeons. Many aeons before, I was a king. Having taken the strong resolution to arrive at supreme perfect enlightenment, my mind did not swerve from its aim; I exerted myself to fulfil the six perfections, bestowing immense alms — gold, gems, villages, towns, provinces, kingdoms, wives, sons, daughters, slaves — up to the sacrifice of life and body, of limbs and members, hands, feet, head; and never did the thought of self-complacency rise in me. In those days the life of men lasted long, and for many hundred thousand years I exercised the rule of a King of the Law for the sake of duty, not for the sake of enjoyment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XI 'Apparition of a Stupa' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: After installing the eldest prince in government I went in quest of the best law in the four quarters, and had promulgated with sound of bell this proclamation: he who procures for me the best law, or points out what is useful, to him will I become a servant. At that time there lived a Seer, who told me: noble king, there is a Sutra called the Lotus of the True Law, an exposition of the best law; if thou consent to become my servant, I will teach thee that law. Glad and exulting, I agreed to do for him the work of a servant, and so I performed the duties of a servitor — fetching grass, fuel, water, bulbs, roots, fruit — and held the office of a doorkeeper; and when I had done such work at day-time, I at night kept his feet while he was lying on his couch, never feeling fatigue of body or mind. In such occupations I passed a full millennium.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XI (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: Was it another who then was the king? No, monks, it was myself. And was it another who was the Seer? No — it was this Devadatta himself, the monk. Indeed, Devadatta was my good friend; by the aid of Devadatta have I accomplished the six perfect virtues, the thirty-two signs of a great man, the ten powers, and all the Tathagata's qualities. I announce to you, monks, I declare to you: this Devadatta, the monk, shall in an age to come, after immense, innumerable aeons, become a Tathagata named Devaraja in the world Devasopana; his lifetime shall measure twenty intermediate kalpas, he shall preach the law in extension, beings equal to the sands of the Ganges shall through him forsake all evils, and after his complete extinction his true law shall stay twenty intermediate kalpas, his body remaining undivided in a stupa of seven precious substances sixty hundred yojanas in height, which all gods and men shall worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XI (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bodhisattvas Issuing from the Gaps of the Earth (Lotus Sutra)

region.en: The Saha-world, whose earth splits open beneath the sky-stupa of Prabhutaratna (supernatural setting; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 娑婆世界——大地裂開，菩薩從虛空中多寶佛塔下涌出（超自然場景；象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884 (Kern ch. XIV; Kumarajiva's ch. 15)

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: When Bodhisattvas from other worlds offer to preach the Lotus in this realm after the Buddha's death, Sakyamuni refuses: he has here in this Saha-world his own hosts. At his word the earth bursts open on every side, and from the clefts arise countless myriads of Bodhisattvas with gold-coloured bodies and the thirty-two signs, each with a retinue like the sands of sixty Ganges rivers; they salute the two Tathagatas seated in the stupa, while fifty intermediate kalpas pass unnoticed, and Maitreya, baffled, asks whence this unheard-of multitude has come.
summary.zh: 他方菩薩請於佛滅後在此娑婆世界弘通法華，佛不許：我此娑婆自有菩薩眾，數如六十恆河沙。語畢，娑婆世界大地悉皆震裂，從地涌出無量千萬億菩薩，金色之身、三十二相，各攜眷屬，多者如六十恆河沙之數；漸次涌出，禮拜虛空中二佛並坐之多寶塔，經五十中劫而大眾如一瞬；彌勒菩薩惑然問佛：此無量菩薩從何所來？

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); scripture material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Out of the multitude of Bodhisattvas who had flocked from other worlds, some eight times equal to the sands of the river Ganges rose from the assembled circle and, stretching out their joined hands, asked leave to proclaim the Dharmaparyaya in this Saha-world after the extinction of the Lord. The Lord answered: Nay, young men of good family, why should you occupy yourselves with this task? I have here in this Saha-world thousands of Bodhisattvas equal to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers, who at the last period after my extinction shall keep, read and proclaim this Dharmaparyaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIV 'Issuing of Bodhisattvas from the Gaps of the Earth' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: No sooner had the Lord uttered these words than the Saha-world burst open on every side, and from within the clefts arose many hundred thousand myriads of kotis of Bodhisattvas with gold-coloured bodies and the thirty-two characteristic signs of a great man, who had been staying in the element of ether underneath this great earth, close to this Saha-world. Each of these Bodhisattvas had a train of thousands of Bodhisattvas similar to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers; there were those with a train equal to the sands of fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, ten, five, four, three, two Ganges rivers; those with a single follower; and those standing isolated — they cannot be numbered, counted or calculated, the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the gaps of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: After they had successively emerged they went up to the stupa of precious substances which stood in the sky, where the Lord Prabhutaratna, the extinct Tathagata, was seated along with the Lord Sakyamuni on the throne; they saluted the feet of both Tathagatas and of the images of Tathagatas produced from the Lord Sakyamuni's body, circumambulated them, celebrated them with hymns, and kept themselves at a little distance with joined hands. While they were saluting, fifty intermediate kalpas in full rolled away, during which the Lord Sakyamuni and the four classes of the audience remained silent; then the Lord produced such an effect of magical power that the four classes fancied it had been no more than one afternoon. Then the four chiefest of that host — Vishesvaritra, Anantaviritra, Vimalakritaviritra and Supratishthitaviritra — asked whether the Lord was in health and the creatures docile; and Maitreya, with the eight hundred thousand myriads of Bodhisattvas like the sands of the Ganges, questioned the Lord in amazement: we never yet saw so great a host; whence have these Bodhisattvas come?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Physician and his Poisoned Sons (Lotus Sutra)

region.en: The Buddha's disclosure of his incalculably long lifetime, told as a family of sick children (symbolic pin — Ganges valley)
region.zh: 佛自宣久遠壽量，以病子之家為喻（象徵性定位——恆河流域）

texts.period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884 (Kern ch. XV 'Duration of Life of the Tathagata'; Kumarajiva's ch. 16)

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: The Buddha announces that he attained enlightenment countless aeons ago and that his apparent extinction is a device: a skilled physician returns from a journey to find his many sons poisoned and rolling on the ground; those of right notions take his remedy, but the perverted refuse it, so he leaves again and lets word go out that he is dead. Bereft, the sons drink the medicine and are cured; the father returns. Even so, says the Buddha, I announce final extinction though I do not become finally extinct — lest beings, seeing me too often, should cease to prize the apparition of a Tathagata — and men of perverted minds worship relics without seeing that in this very place he continues preaching the law.
summary.zh: 佛自言：成佛已來無量無邊劫，所說示滅皆為教化眾生之權巧。譬如良醫離家，諸子誤飲毒藥，號呼輾轉；醫還，搗合良藥令服，中其心者即愈；心智錯亂者不肯服。醫父便設方便：告諸子言我老病死，棄之他國，遣使還報訃音；諸子聞父背寢，悲悼惶怖，遂肯服藥，毒病皆愈。醫父知子病醒，便還歸家相見。佛言：我亦如是，成佛已來無量劫，為度眾生故方便示現涅槃，而實不滅——眾生見我常在，便生憍恣，不肯勤求；故示滅度，使生戀慕。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); scripture material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved. Comparative parallel: the pretended death that saves belongs to the resurrection cluster of the wider corpus (the returned saviour wrongly believed dead).

passages.text: Let us suppose an analogous case, said the Buddha. There is some physician, learned, intelligent, prudent, clever in allaying all sorts of diseases, who has many sons, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred. The physician once being abroad, all his children incur a disease from poison or venom; overcome with grievous pains they lie rolling on the ground. Their father comes home at the time when his sons are suffering; some of them have perverted notions, others right notions, but all suffer the same pain. On seeing their father they cheerfully greet him: hail, dear father, that thou art come back in safety; now deliver us from our evil and let us live!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XV 'Duration of Life of the Tathagata' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The physician prepares a great remedy with the required colour, smell and taste, pounds it on a stone, and gives it to his sons: take this, and you shall soon be rid of the poison and be healthy. Those among the children who have right notions take it quickly and are soon totally delivered from their disease; but the sons with perverted notions do not take the remedy offered, because owing to the perverseness of their notions it does not please them in colour, smell nor taste. Then the physician reflects: these sons of mine have become perverted in their notions owing to the poison, since they do not take the remedy; therefore will I by some able device induce them to take it. He says to them: I am old, decrepit, advanced in years, and my term of life is near at hand; here have I prepared a great remedy for you — and skilfully betakes himself to another part of the country, letting his sick sons know that he has departed life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: They are extremely sorry and bewail him: so then he is dead, our father and protector, he who begat us, he so full of bounty! now are we left without a protector. Fully aware of their being orphans and having no refuge, they are plunged in sorrow, by which their perverted notions make room for right notions; they acknowledge that the remedy has the required colour, smell and taste, instantly take it, and are delivered from their evil. Then, on knowing that these sons are delivered, the physician shows himself again. In the same manner, says the Buddha, I have arrived at supreme perfect enlightenment since an immense incalculable number of aeons; but from time to time I display such able devices to the creatures with the view of educating them, without there being in that respect any falsehood on my part — for I see how the creatures are afflicted, but I do not show them my proper being; let them first have an aspiration to see me, then I will reveal to them the true law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Sada-paribhuta, the Bodhisattva who Never Disparaged (Lotus Sutra)

region.en: The world Mahasambhava in the aeon Vinirbhoga, under the Buddha Bhishmagarjitasvararaja (supernatural setting; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 威音王如來之世，大離車世界（超自然場景；象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884 (Kern ch. XIX 'Sada-paribhuta'; Kumarajiva's ch. 20)

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: In the age when the counterfeit of the law was fading and proud monks oppressed its reign, there was a monk-Bodhisattva who taught nothing but one refrain: to every monk, nun and lay devotee he cried 'I do not contemn you, worthies! You deserve no contempt, for you all observe the course of duty of Bodhisattvas and are to become Tathagatas.' For years they abused him, threw clods and sticks, and nicknamed him Sada-paribhuta — 'always contemned.' At his death a voice from the sky expounded the Lotus to him; he gained the six perfections of the senses, vowed to live on, converted all who had reviled him — and the Buddha reveals that he was that bodhisattva himself, while the mockers are the five hundred monks, nuns and lay devotees of this very assembly, who had fallen to hell for their malignity but were ripened by him in the end.
summary.zh: 於威音王佛滅後、像法將盡、增上慢比丘橫行其時，有一比丘菩薩，不行讀誦，唯行一事：逢四眾則禮拜讚歎言：『我不敢輕於汝等，汝等皆行菩薩道，當得作佛。』眾人聞已，或以杖木瓦石擲之，避走而罵，因號之曰常不輕菩薩。臨命終時，於虛空中聞威音王佛廣說法華二十千萬億偈，得六根清淨，更增壽命，普為罵者說法，令住菩提。佛言：常不輕菩薩者，則我身是；爾時罵打彼者——今此會中五百菩薩、五百比丘尼、五百優婆塞是，彼以宿罵故，於墮惡道受苦，今得值佛，住不退轉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); scripture material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: After the complete extinction of the first of the Tathagatas called Bhishmagarjitasvararaja, when his true law had disappeared and the counterfeit of the true law was fading, when the reign of the law was being oppressed by proud monks, there was a monk, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva, called Sada-paribhuta. He was called so because he was in the habit of exclaiming to every monk or nun, male or female lay devotee, while approaching them: I do not contemn you, worthies; you deserve no contempt, for you all observe the course of duty of Bodhisattvas and are to become Tathagatas. That Bodhisattva at that time did not teach nor study; the only thing he did was, whenever he descried from afar a monk or nun or lay devotee, to approach and exclaim thus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIX 'Sada-paribhuta' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: But all were extremely irritated and angry at it, showed him their displeasure, abused and insulted him: why does he, unasked, declare that he feels no contempt for us? Just by so doing he shows a contempt for us; he renders himself contemptible by predicting our future destiny; we do not care for what is not true. Many years went on during which the Bodhisattva was being abused, but he was not angry at anybody, nor felt malignity; and to those who cast a clod or stick at him, he loudly exclaimed from afar: I do not contemn you. Those monks, nuns and lay devotees, always addressed in that phrase, gave him the nickname of Sada-paribhuta — both 'always contemned' and 'never contemned.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIX (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the end of his life the Bodhisattva happened to hear this Dharmaparyaya of the Lotus of the True Law: it was the Lord Bhishmagarjitasvararaja who expounded it in twenty times twenty hundred thousand myriads of stanzas, which the Bodhisattva heard from a voice in the sky as death drew near. On hearing that voice he grasped the Dharmaparyaya, obtained the perfection of sight, hearing, smell, taste, body and mind, made a vow to prolong his life for twenty hundred thousand myriads of years, and promulgated the Lotus to the four classes. And all those proud beings who had given him the nickname became his followers when they saw the strength of his sublime magic faculties; the Buddha declares: he who at that time was the Bodhisattva Sada-paribhuta was myself, and those who hooted at him are the five hundred Bodhisattvas headed by Bhadrapala, the five hundred nuns and the five hundred lay devotees of this very assembly, who, for their malignity, never saw a Tathagata for twenty hundred thousand myriads of aeons and suffered terrible pain in the great hell Avici — and thereafter were all brought by him to full ripeness for supreme perfect enlightenment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIX (Kern 1884); not verbatim.
